extracted.intended_audience: European patent applicants, patent attorneys, and EPO examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a European patent application discloses the invention sufficiently clearly and completely for a person skilled in the art to carry it out, including assessment standards and special-case requirements (AI, biological material).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 83 EPC general requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The European patent application (or patent) shall disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for it to be carried out by a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core sufficiency obligation: the description plus any examples/drawings must enable practice of the invention. Use the language of the EPC as the primary test when assessing sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement over the whole scope of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure must be reproducible without undue burden, and this must be true over the whole scope of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the skilled person can carry out the invention across the entire claimed range. If parts of the claim cannot be practiced without undue experimentation, those claim portions may be insufficiently disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skilled person / common general knowledge standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must contain sufficient information to allow a person skilled in the art, using common general knowledge and the information provided in the application, to perceive the technical teaching inherent in the claimed invention and put it into effect accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment combines what is disclosed in the application with what the skilled person already knows. Do not require disclosure of what is routine for the skilled person, but do require anything necessary beyond common general knowledge to practice the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 42(1)(e) — describe at least one way and use examples/drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: The description shall: describe in detail at least one way of carrying out the invention claimed; use examples where appropriate; refer to the drawings, if any.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the specification gives at least one concrete embodiment or working example and points to drawings where relevant. Lack of any concrete way of carrying out the invention is a key sufficiency weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for assessment and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection of lack of sufficient disclosure presupposes that there are serious doubts, substantiated by verifiable facts. If the examining division can make out a reasoned case, the onus shifts to the applicant to establish that the invention may be performed and repeated over substantially the whole of the claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For examiners: raise objections only when there are verifiable facts creating serious doubts and explain them in a reasoned case. For applicants: be prepared to furnish counter-evidence or amendments to show reproducibility across the claimed range once a reasoned case is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: No undue burden / no inventive skill required to carry out
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must allow the skilled person to perform the invention over the whole area claimed without undue burden and without needing inventive skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If practicing the invention would itself require inventive activity (new inventive steps), this indicates insufficiency. Look for guidance, parameters, and working conditions that prevent undue trial-and-error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility of technical effect (G 2/21)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical effects relied upon for inventive step must be derivable from the application as filed; bald assertions are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an inventive-step argument depends on a technical effect, the specification must make that effect at least plausible (e.g., by data, examples, or a credible technical explanation). Mere unsubstantiated claims of effect risk insufficiency or loss of support for inventive-step arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI inventions — disclosure of training data and model details (T 1669/21)
rubrics_metrics.description: For AI-related inventions, training data, model architecture, and hyperparameters may need to be disclosed if necessary to reproduce the technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'black-box' AI disclosures skeptically: if reproduction of the claimed technical effect depends on model internals or training data, the application should disclose those elements or sufficient alternatives so a skilled person can reproduce the effect without undue burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological materials — deposit requirement (Budapest Treaty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where biological material cannot be sufficiently described, deposit at a recognized depository (Budapest Treaty) is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a biological invention cannot be made reproducible by description alone, ensure a deposit is made and correctly referenced in the application; otherwise the disclosure may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from Articles 84 (clarity) and 56 (inventive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 83: whole disclosure enables practice (sufficiency); Article 84: claims are clear and supported (clarity); Article 56: invention is non-obvious (inventive step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate lack of clarity or lack of inventive step with lack of sufficiency. Evaluate sufficiency on whether the invention can be performed as claimed, separately from clarity of claim wording or the inventive-step assessment.
